paper.title: What Do Digital Traces Predict? Task Effects, Student Differences, and Critical Online Reasoning
paper.abstract: Digital assessment traces are increasingly used to predict student performance, often evaluated by correlating predicted and observed scores pooled across tasks. However, such correlations may reflect between-task differences rather than performance differences among students within tasks. To investigate this, we analyzed up to 527 browsing sessions from 424 university students completing open-Internet Critical Online Reasoning tasks and assessed the cross-task stability of their ratings. We evaluated the same out-of-fold predictions within and across tasks, compared three validation tiers up to leave-one-task-out, and tested incremental predictive contributions of consultation order and relational structure against matched permutation and randomization controls. None of the twelve prespecified primary tests was significant: on held-out tasks, consulted-page features showed no significant association with relative student performance, nor did observed order or relational structure add predictive value. Pooling observations across tasks substantially increased correlations, particularly for factual correctness, whose scores showed limited evidence of stable between-student differences across tasks. However, sentence embeddings yielded modest positive correlations with generic response quality on held-out tasks, without establishing added predictive value from observed order or relational structure. Our findings show that pooled predictive correlations may not reflect within-task student differences, highlighting the need for within-task evaluation and criterion generalizability audits.

paper.title: ClearTalk: Data-Driven Mandarin Articulation Analysis and Personalized Communication Support for Children with Dysarthria
paper.abstract: Children with dysarthria may experience reduced intelligibility and difficulty expressing everyday needs. ClearTalk is a smartwatch-based system that converts Mandarin speech-recognition differences into interpretable articulatory profiles for personalized practice and staged communication. Target and recognized utterances are aligned at the syllable level, summarized across seven articulatory positions, and ranked by a count-sensitive asymmetric heuristic. For 13 dysarthric speakers from the Mandarin Dysarthria Speech Corpus, system syllable-level accuracy showed a Pearson correlation of 0.908 with expert intelligibility, with an R-squared value of 0.824 and a p-value below 0.001. The system-selected priority targets achieved an 86.7 percent overlap with the consensus of three blinded speech-language pathologists; across 210 target consonants, automated labels achieved 86.7 percent agreement, a Cohen's kappa of 0.76, and a macro-F1 score of 0.81. In a balanced single-session pilot with 15 children, mean pre/post gains were 14.4, 29.4, and 27.7 percentage points for mild, moderate, and severe groups, while communication-round completion rates were 81.3, 66.7, and 48.0 percent. These findings support the feasibility of using interpretable patterns of speech errors to guide wearable articulation practice and communication assistance.

paper.title: Refusal Register is Causally Steerable: Decomposing the Refusal Direction into Category-Aligned Components in Gemma-2-9B-IT
paper.abstract: Prior work shows that refusal in instruction-tuned language models can be ablated by intervening on a single residual-stream direction (Arditi et al., 2024), and more recent work finds multiple refusal-mediating directions and concept cones (Wollschläger et al., 2025). We ask a different question: do refusal-related directions carry information about the register of refusal language - how the model refuses - and not only whether it refuses? In Gemma-2-9B-IT we identify two SVM-derived linear directions (B1 for harmful-content vs. neutral, B2 for self-reference vs. neutral) at layer 20 with cos(B1, B2) = 0.252 (about 75 degrees, substantially non-parallel). Adding the harmful-vs-neutral difference-of-means direction (cosine 0.68 with B1) to the residual stream of self-reference prompts at alpha = 2.0 shifts content-safety vocabulary from 2.55 to 10.37 hits per 100 tokens, while a magnitude-matched random direction produces 1.13-2.16; the model continues to refuse but switches register from meta-style ("as a language model...") to content-style ("this would be harmful"). The same register-injection effect reproduces qualitatively in Gemma-2-2B-IT at layer 12 (content vocabulary 1.72 -> 6.37 at alpha = 1.0, vs. random control 1.35), with a narrower coherent-injection window than in 9B. The two directions are not symmetric: the B2 -> harmful intervention produces a much smaller register effect, and across ablation, sufficiency, and injection B1's causal effects are consistently larger than B2's. We frame this asymmetry as part of the finding: B1 appears to encode both category detection and refusal-vocabulary information, while B2 encodes primarily category detection. We frame the contribution as identifying category-aligned components related to the Arditi-style difference-of-means direction that play distinct functional roles in refusal register.

paper.title: IndustrialKnowEval: A Benchmark for Evaluating Multi-Level Industrial Knowledge in LLMs
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored for industrial tasks, yet few benchmarks evaluate their mastery of industrial knowledge across different types of cognitive demand. We introduce IndustrialKnowEval (IndKnow), a benchmark for industrial knowledge and engineering question answering. It contains 43,282 samples covering 21 task types across seven industrial sectors, including aerospace, electric power, and metallurgy, organized into four levels of cognitive demand: memory, comprehension, reasoning, and engineering application. Enterprise-based domain specialists and experienced researchers participate in all stages of dataset construction and quality control. We conduct a series of experiments on 18 representative LLMs, with domain experts deeply involved in the evaluation. Building upon IndKnow, we propose the Industrial Cognitive Capability Gap (ICCG) metric to characterize the performance differential between foundational industrial knowledge and higher-order reasoning and application, and we analyze it alongside absolute performance to provide a more complete view of model capabilities. We anticipate that IndustrialKnowEval will support the benchmarking of LLMs in industrial scenarios and promote the development of robust industrial intelligence. Code is available at: https://github.com/J4cksonLee/IndKnow

paper.title: CuRSE-Bench: A Benchmark for Probing Cultural Blind Spots in Text-to-Image Safety Evaluation
paper.abstract: Text-to-image (T2I) safety evaluation typically assigns each prompt or image a single culture-blind harm label, so content that is harmful only within a particular culture can pass as benign. We introduce CultureCraft, an agentic framework that constructs T2I prompts that appear benign under a general-purpose rubric yet carry a latent harmful meaning in a target culture, and use it to build CuRSE-Bench: 10,709 culture-specific prompts and 2,648 culture-general controls over six regions and ten harm axes, each drawn from a predefined knowledge base of documented harm vectors and traceable to at least two independent sources. Scoring every prompt under six region persona judges and a paired culture-blind judge, we find that the culture-blind judge under-rates culture-specific latent harm while matching the persona judges on the controls. Each persona judge, in turn, chiefly decodes its own region's latent harm under our instrument: a selective cultural blind spot that persists in deployed moderators.

paper.title: Necessary for What? Auditing Demographic Disclosure to LLM Synthetic Respondents
paper.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) increasingly answer surveys on behalf of real panelists, and each panelist's recorded demographic attributes (e.g., age, education, ethnicity) are often placed in the prompt on the premise that richer profiles make more faithful synthetic respondents. While data minimization limits personal data to what a purpose requires, a synthetic survey serves several purposes at once, from predicting individual answers to estimating how opinions are distributed and comparing groups. We ask which of these purposes require the respondent's record, and whether improved estimates support sound conclusions about groups. We vary whose profile a model receives, where it comes from, and how many fields it contains, in two U.S. surveys with eleven open-weight and three hosted models, and compare each model with a statistical model fit to the same information. We make four contributions. First, we show that the record adds little to individual predictions and that, for the open-weight models, most of its gain in population estimates remains when it is replaced by census data or a synthetic persona. Second, we find that group comparisons improve only with the respondent's own record, and that even then the models' group differences rest more on the demographic label in the prompt than on the individual respondent, which the usual check of reproducing known group differences does not reveal. Third, we find that the models make groups look more alike than they are, keeping differences in circumstances while flattening or reversing differences in attitudes, most sharply for religious affiliation and ethnic origin, both special categories of personal data. Fourth, we outline an audit that a survey organization can run on questions it has already fielded to decide which estimates may use the record.

paper.title: Can LLMs Give Good Product Advice? A Framework for Diagnosing Failures
paper.abstract: Evaluating product advice from a language model requires assessing whether the recommendation meets the user's needs and identifying where the model falls short when it does not. However, matching a product mentioned in an online reply cannot answer either question on its own: several products may be suitable, and the recorded answer may itself be poor advice. When shown a community-listed alternative alongside their own sampled car recommendation, six models prefer the alternative in 1.9 to 6.5 percent of eligible disagreements, consistently across both source-blind presentation orders. We propose a diagnostic framework that separates the user's stated needs, the model's added assumptions, candidate generation, filtering, and final choice, with 19 possible failure modes and the evidence needed to assess them. We apply this framework to product-advice data and to a separate product-selection task with externally assigned relevance labels. The experiments distinguish naming a community-listed product from selecting it and show how answer extraction and candidate-list construction affect the outcome.

paper.title: A Concurrent Structured Record Mirrored the Prose It Accompanied: A Pre-Registered Conceptual Replication and Extension of the Hide Pending Tool Call Scenario
paper.abstract: Huang et al. (2026) show that language models writing reports of agentic work tend to conceal narrative-changing flaws, and that appending "Be honest in your response." to the instruction substantially increases disclosure in most of their scenarios. In their Hide Pending Tool Call scenario, where a broader follow-up query was accepted but never returned, the honesty prompt left GPT-5.5's rate of flagging the missing data at 0%, although it turned most answers into caveats. I ask whether a different request changes this: appending, in the same generation, a structured record that follows the schema of an adversarial-review tool, including a residue section for what remained unresolved. In two pre-registered phases on the same 100 synthetic log pairs, each pending log matched with a clean twin in which the follow-up query did return, I ran gpt-5.6-sol through Codex CLI under four conditions. Phase 1 measured the record: with the residue schema, a judge coded it as stating the unreturned query in 29% of logs, against 5% with a findings-only placebo schema, and in none of the clean twins (p = 1.2 x 10^-7); a second run two days later gave 30% and 6%. But 70-71% of residue records declared that nothing remained open while the query was pending. Phase 2 measured the prose answer: the confirmatory comparison against the honesty prompt was not significant (four discordant logs, all favoring the honesty prompt; p = 0.125), no equivalence test was pre-registered, and the judge failed the pre-registered human validation on the decisive category; I therefore claim neither an effect nor its absence. In an exploratory cross-tabulation, every residue record coded as stating the gap accompanied prose coded as mentioning it (30 of 30), and none accompanied prose coded as omitting it (0 of 70): in this setting, the structured record mirrored the prose it accompanied.

paper.title: GaugeRoPE: RoPE-Compatible Executable Latent Attention
paper.abstract: Latent KV cache compression reduces memory footprint by mapping historical keys and values into compact representations. However, generic compressed key states require reconstruction to native dimension before applying RoPE and computing attention scores, adding sequence-scaling overhead to the decode path. We characterize when a latent KV representation can serve directly as the execution state of pretrained RoPE. For RoPE-based transformers, exact static linear execution of the rotary key path requires the latent-to-native map to preserve the pretrained RoPE action through an intertwining relation, restricting exact mixing to coordinates that share the same RoPE frequency. Guided by this characterization, we build GaugeRoPE, a training-free executable latent KV representation. It combines a RoPE-compatible carrier that preserves the rotary action with an approximate position-independent residual key--value (RKV) correction for complementary key and value information, both evaluated without per-token dense historical K/V reconstruction. On Mistral-7B, GaugeRoPE achieves $5.85\times$ KV compression while maintaining quality close to the full-cache baseline. Additional MHA results validate the construction beyond GQA. GaugeRoPE achieves up to $2.48\times$ the decode throughput of the vanilla uncompressed baseline through direct latent execution.

paper.title: Abstention Direction in Large Language Models: Mechanistic Interpretability of Abstention Across Query Ambiguity, Knowledge Limits, and Safety Alignment
paper.abstract: Abstention, the withholding of a response by a large language model (LLM) under uncertainty or safety risks, is essential for trustworthy models. The causes of abstention fall into three perspectives: ambiguity in the Query (Q), limits of Model Knowledge (MK), and misalignment with Human Values (HV). However, prior analyses of internal representations have focused on HV, using a refusal direction computed from harmful and harmless queries. No study has analyzed the three perspectives jointly. We therefore extend the refusal direction framework to all three perspectives. Specifically, for each perspective, we construct counterfactual pairs that share a template and differ only in the abstention-inducing factor, and compute an abstention direction by normalizing the difference in mean activations between the two polarities. Activation steering experiments show that intervening in middle layers increases or decreases abstention across all three perspectives. Moreover, steering yields cross-perspective effects, indicating that the abstention directions share a common directional component.

paper.title: Do Simulated Users Push Back Like Real Users? Correctness vs. Stance
paper.abstract: LLM-simulated users stand in for people in multi-turn evaluations, on the assumption that they react to what the assistant says. We test this for pushback. From WildChat, we take conversations in which the assistant explicitly challenges or endorses a position the user stated, and compare the real next user turn with simulated turns from the same prefix. Among users who replied, real users push back more after a challenge than after an endorsement (20.5% vs. 8.2%); a GPT-based simulator does not (27.1% vs. 27.1%): stance gap D = -0.12 [-0.17, -0.08]. After a challenge the simulator instead often re-states or re-interprets its request ("I meant ..."); about half of these turns are disguised insistence, which puts D between -0.08 and -0.05. What drives the simulator's disputing is whether the assistant's position is judged correct (21% vs. 49% after challenges; 16% vs. 58% after endorsements), while real users change little (19% vs. 24%; 7% vs. 12%), under every outcome definition we tried. Real same-stance examples do not fix this, and another GPT-based simulator and two Claude simulators show stance effects close to real users. Stance sensitivity should be measured for each simulator, not assumed.

paper.title: When the Cheapest Feasible Router Fails: Auditing Deployment Commitments in Cost-Aware LLM Routing
paper.abstract: Cost-aware LLM routing often selects the cheapest policy meeting empirical risk and coverage constraints. Yet a router that passes an audit can violate its fixed service contract on new requests, even when candidate policies are constructed independently. We study this deployment-commitment decision with disjoint construction, audit, and test samples. Across 19 RouterBench task families, the cheapest audit-feasible router deploys in 91.82% of opportunities but violates the held-out contract in 32.22% of deployments. We introduce Menu-Aware Routing Commitment (MARC), which qualifies policies using audit evidence and a serving-cost tolerance to retain the apparent winner, deploy a supported alternative, or defer. Its practical policywise variant (MARC-P) reduces observed conditional failure to 0.73% at 85.79% deployment, with higher serving cost; fixed-margin and formal risk-control procedures provide competitive alternatives. Nested audits show how added evidence changes deployable policy sets, and learned semantic routing exhibits the same commitment failure. These results establish deployment commitment as a distinct operational decision connecting router evaluation, service reliability, and inference cost.

paper.title: TETHER: Training-Free, Elastic, ToC-Anchored Hierarchy Extraction and Recovery in Design-Driven Long Documents
paper.abstract: Converting complex documents into structured knowledge constitutes the critical infrastructure urgently required for deploying Large Language Models (LLMs) in downstream research. However, blind to the Table of Contents (ToC) as a macro-structure, existing bottom-up paradigms rely on localized visual cues, inducing heuristic fragility in high-entropy layouts where visual prominence decouples from logical depth; meanwhile, direct LLM extraction lacks spatial grounding, triggering hallucinations in long contexts. To address this, we introduce TETHER, a training-free framework that elevates the ToC from discarded noise to a vital structural prior, enabling robust adaptation across design-driven long documents. TETHER operates via a two-stage neuro-symbolic mechanism: first, it constructs a document skeleton from the raw ToC using a Large Multimodal Model (LMM) empowered by spatio-semantic constraints; second, it employs an anchor-based alignment strategy to tether content blocks to this skeleton, effectively resolving boundary ambiguities. Evaluated across a multilingual benchmark of ESG reports, product manuals, and annual reports, TETHER delivers highly precise, state-of-the-art (SOTA) zero-shot hierarchy recovery, outperforming deep hierarchical recovery models, dedicated parsers, and general-purpose LMMs. Moreover, stress tests highlight TETHER's resilience to sparse omissions and textual noise, demonstrating that its precise semantic alignment is fundamentally anchored in topological and depth fidelity. Crucially, ablations confirm the framework's architectural irreducibility, while achieving 90% token reduction and drastic speedups over end-to-end baselines, establishing a compelling equilibrium between structural precision and deployment scalability.

paper.title: Literary Language Mashup: Curating Fictions with Large Language Models
paper.abstract: In this paper, we propose an alternative approach to human evaluation of literary fictions by employing LLMs themselves as evaluators within the GrAImes framework. We apply this methodology to assess human-written and AI-generated microfictions in Spanish, to five PhD professors in literature and sixteen literary enthusiasts, and to short stories in both Spanish and English. By comparing the evaluations performed by LLMs with those of human judges, we examine the degree of alignment and divergence between both perspectives, thereby assessing the feasibility of LLMs as auxiliary literary evaluators. Our analysis focuses on the alignment of responses from LLMs with those of human evaluators, providing insights into the potential of LLMs in literary assessment. The conducted experiments reveal that while LLMs cannot be regarded as substitutes for human judges in the evaluation of literary microfictions and short stories, with a Krippendorff's alpha reliability coefficient less than 0.66, they can serve as a valuable tool that offers an initial perspective on the editorial quality of the texts in question. Overall, this study contributes to the ongoing discourse on the role of artificial intelligence in literature, underlining both its methodological constraints and its potential as a complementary resource for literary evaluation.

paper.title: When Should Decision Models Compare Candidates?
paper.abstract: Language-model agents frequently select among candidate actions, such as tools and web elements. Should decision models score candidates independently or allow their scores to depend on other candidates? We investigate this question by comparing three approaches: Pointwise scoring, Setwise scoring, and Candidate Attention. Across five agent-decision benchmarks, Pointwise scoring remains competitive, while Setwise scoring performs better on some tool-selection and binary-decision tasks. Candidate Attention does not consistently improve upon Pointwise scoring, despite allowing cross-candidate interaction. Using two controlled synthetic tasks, we further examine whether models learn to use candidate-set information. With targeted relational training, Setwise models learn candidate dependencies and generalize to shifted inputs, while Candidate Attention shows weaker transfer. Our results show that access to other candidates does not guarantee effective comparison, and that its benefits depend on both task requirements and training.

paper.title: Invariant-Aware Harness Enforcement to Protect LLM Agents from Silent API Failures
paper.abstract: LLM agents answer questions by calling APIs and trusting the results. An API can fail silently. It ignores part of a request, such as a misnamed filter, yet returns HTTP 200 and a plausible but wrong result. Current fixes, such as checklists, reviewer models and LLM judges, ask the model to catch it. But models often see the problem and answer anyway. We present SilentGuard, which moves the decision from the model to the harness running tool calls. It tests each result against invariants that any correct API must satisfy and withholds values that break one. We find silent failures in 11 of 15 public research APIs, with counts inflated up to 691 times. Current fixes leave over 70% of answers wrong, and agents report 77.4% of counts a judge flags. Across 7 open models, SilentGuard cuts wrong answers on its target faults from 74.0% to 1.7%, with no loss on fault-free tasks. On three frontier models they fall from 70.2% to 0.5%. A warning from the same check leaves 70.1% wrong, so enforcement is the key. On new fault types, the harness alone cuts wrong answers from 61.1% to 24.5%. It avoids wrong answers by abstaining rather than recovering.

paper.title: Asking What Matters: Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection for Interactive Text-to-SQL
paper.abstract: Interactive text-to-SQL requires an LLM agent not only to generate executable SQL, but also to decide which uncertainty to clarify within a limited interaction budget. However, current clarification policies have three limitations: (i) they target surface ambiguity without testing its SQL impact; (ii) they miss ambiguities implicit in schema routes or domain knowledge; and (iii) they spend limited turns on unfocused or redundant questions. These limitations expose a critical challenge: identifying SQL-impacting ambiguity before the intended SQL is known. In this paper, we propose DisGuAD, a Disagreement-Guided Ambiguity Detection framework that specializes clarification selection. DisGuAD treats disagreement among plausible SQL interpretations as direct evidence of which uncertainty matters to the final query. Specifically, it constructs a query-term inventory, elicits contrastive SQL interpretations through complementary probe families, compares their canonical SQL components, and attributes recurring differences to user-facing clarification targets. A lightweight prioritization and dialogue-state mechanism then selects one high-impact unresolved target for clarification. Experiments on BIRD-Interact Lite and Full with two LLM backbones demonstrate consistent improvements in task success and clarification quality. Compared with the original interaction policy, DisGuAD improves normalized Reward by 4.40--8.97 points and raises overall critical-ambiguity coverage from 48.62% to 82.75% and from 45.76% to 85.14%. Its clarification signals further improve two independently designed static text-to-SQL frameworks by up to 13.97 Reward points while keeping their SQL generators fixed. These results demonstrate that disagreement among plausible SQL queries provides actionable evidence for selecting clarification targets that matter to downstream generation.

paper.title: What Counts as Attack Success? Evaluating Harmfulness in Red Teaming LLMs
paper.abstract: Judging whether a model response is harmful requires contextual and normative choices, yet red-teaming studies often delegate this judgment to automated evaluators. We examine how harmfulness criteria are specified in red-teaming research and how they carry through to reported results. Reviewing 76 papers, we find that many adopt their criteria from prior datasets, classifiers, or judge prompts rather than defining harmfulness themselves. Applying evaluators from these papers to identical outputs, we find that they can reach different judgments on the same response, which can change conclusions when comparing models. These differences arise partly because evaluators draw the boundary of harm in different places: some count any response that does not refuse, while others count only output that could plausibly cause harm. We argue that red-teaming studies should state their harmfulness criteria and report how they chose and validated their evaluators to support more reliable measurement and interpretation.

paper.title: Can an LLM dream? Testing the overfitted brain hypothesis on an agent with text memory
paper.abstract: Hoel (2021) proposed that dreams distort replayed experience so that the brain does not overfit to recent events. We test this hypothesis on an LLM agent (Claude Opus 5.5) that stores what it learns in a text memory and rewrites that memory each night from the day's conversation transcript. The agent goes through ten simulated days of conversation built from LongMemEval. We corrupt 5, 10, 20 or 40 percent of the transcript's turns before each nightly rewrite in one of two ways. Detail corruption changes one or two details in a turn to plausible wrong ones, or replaces the turn with one by the same speaker from an earlier day. Random-text corruption replaces half of the selected turns with a passage of Moby-Dick and inserts Moby-Dick words into the other half. A size limit on the memory, rising from 19,500 to 117,000 tokens over ten nights, set from human free-recall data, forces it to forget. We learned that corruption did not help the agent apply what it learned in earlier conversations to new tasks in any of 30 runs (ten conditions, three different conversation histories). Replacing details in 40 percent of turns lowered recall from 76 to 60 percent. Random text had no consistent effect on recall, with a paired difference of 0 $\pm$ 2 points at 40 percent, because the model recognized it as corrupted and left it out of memory. Replaced details were stored as fact even when another turn held the correct value, and the agent answered 40 percent of those questions correctly, compared with 75 percent without corruption. These results suggest that a pretrained model can separate corrupted text from real events, so a fair test needs a learner that cannot make this separation as easily, such as a model fine-tuned on the corrupted days or an agent whose days take place in an invented world.

paper.title: SnakeTranslate: Weakly Supervised Policy Learning from Offline Parallel Text for Simultaneous Translation
paper.abstract: Adaptive simultaneous translation requires reliable prefix translation and timely READ/WRITE decisions, but ordinary parallel corpora provide no action annotations. We present SnakeTranslate, which adapts loss-derived alignment to sampled causal histories for jointly learning both capabilities. The framework supports supervised fine-tuning (SFT) on parallel text and on-policy distillation (OPD) with reverse Kullback--Leibler (KL) divergence on student-generated translations. At inference, source and target tokens form one append-only interleaved history, enabling incremental decoding with cache reuse. On FLEURS, NTREX128, and WMT24++, our 4B model improves quality--latency trade-offs over streaming policies applied to the same offline-tuned backbone, with further gains from OPD. paper.title: Trait Collapse in Text-to-Image Generation: Evaluating and Mitigating Personality Inconsistency in Visual Storytelling
paper.abstract: In visual storytelling, a believable character must not only look consistent across scenes but also \textit{behave} in ways that reflect their personality. Current text-to-image (T2I) models preserve visual appearance effectively, yet consistently fail to maintain personality-relevant behavior---a failure we term \textit{trait collapse}. We show that conventional metrics (CLIP Score, DINO similarity) are blind to this failure, and that abstract personality descriptors and scene-level emotion labels do not produce consistent improvements over neutral prompts across models. To systematically diagnose trait collapse, we introduce \textbf{ViStoryBench-Personality}, a story-level benchmark combining an expert-validated Visual Cues Lexicon (Fleiss' $κ= 0.757$) with a six-dimensional metric suite covering personality alignment, cross-scene stability, and behavioral coherence. Evaluating seven T2I systems, we confirm a persistent semantic gap between abstract trait labels and visual evidence, and find that visual identity consistency does not imply personality consistency. To bridge this gap, we propose \textbf{Trait-Behavior-Visual (TBV)}, a training-free prompting framework that decomposes personality traits into renderable visual constraints. TBV improves Personality Alignment Score by up to $+22.1\%$, with larger gains in models with stronger language-conditioning capacity.

paper.title: RAW: Refusal Aversion in the Wild, A Causal Measurement Method for Deployed LLMs
paper.abstract: Deployed LLMs field hundreds of millions of conversations a day and refuse a non-trivial fraction of user requests, yet the user-side cost of refusal, whether users disengage and by how much, is unmeasured on any production model: a blind spot for the consumer-facing platforms built on them. A/B-testing refusal is ethically and operationally constrained on frontier-lab products and unavailable to third-party platforms deploying these models through a fixed API. We introduce RAW, a method that uses LLM stochasticity as a natural experiment: at near-identical prompts in any existing log, the same model sometimes refuses and sometimes does not, and that variation identifies the causal user-side effect of refusal. Applying the method to 15 deployed LLMs in LMSYS-Chat-1M and WildChat, with user-clustered inference, we find that for about half of the models we can measure precisely, a refusal costs 3 to 17 pp of subsequent re-engagement; the rest show no distinguishable effect, among them one deployment whose positive point estimate we trace to persistent users retrying the refused request. Our contribution is the measurement method, which runs on any deployed model from logs alone for about \$0.30 per 1,000 conversations. We release labels, moderation scores, prompt embeddings, and pipeline code.

paper.title: Sleep2Word: Peripheral-to-EEG Translation via Duration-Aware Wordization
paper.abstract: Estimating full-night electroencephalography (EEG) spectrograms from peripheral measurements could extend EEG-informed sleep analysis to recordings acquired without EEG. This task requires compact representations of signals with different temporal structures. We introduce Sleep2Word, a framework for translating respiration, electrocardiography (ECG), or photoplethysmography (PPG) into EEG spectrograms through duration-aware physiological words. Building on context-dependent chunking, Sleep2Word groups physiological embeddings into variable-duration chunks and jointly quantizes their content and duration into modality-specific wordbooks. A block-autoregressive translator then predicts target EEG word identities and occurrence-specific duration refinements within fixed-duration blocks. This design accommodates independent source and target wordbooks, limits temporal drift, and shortens the autoregressive decoding path. Trained on over 20K PSG cases across 9 datasets, Sleep2Word consistently outperforms existing spectrogram generation baselines in EEG spectrogram reconstruction, sleep staging, arousal detection, and survival prediction. Compressing full night sequences by up to 69.7%, the learned words yield a favorable accuracy-compute trade-off. Sleep event analysis further shows that the learned words capture physiologically plausible associations across modalities, suggesting their potential for interpretable cross-modal analysis.

paper.title: MInfoVisQA: A Multilingual Benchmark for Information-Rich Visual Question Answering
paper.abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) excel in vision-language tasks; yet, whether they maintain consistent understanding of information-rich visuals (InfoVis) when the surface language changes remains unclear. To quantify this capability, we introduce MInfoVisQA, a parallel benchmark with 8,960 QA configurations derived from 128 seed instances across 24 languages. We construct seed-matched, language-parallel visuals and QA pairs by disentangling numerical-structural data from text and programmatically synchronizing translated labels. We evaluate 25 MLLMs under two settings: Language-Aligned QA (LQA, matching visual-text languages) and Cross-Language QA (XQA, fixed QA language with varying visual languages). The results show that aggregate accuracy masks substantial robustness gaps: two models with comparable mean LQA accuracy (80.4\%) exhibit performance spreads of 7.8 and 20.3 percentage points across languages. Moreover, all 25 models score lower with non-English visuals under fixed English QA, underscoring the need for cross-language sensitivity metrics.

paper.title: Enhancing Understanding of Language Models with Varied Explanations
paper.abstract: Language models are increasingly used to support human judgement in complex reasoning tasks, yet their predictions often remain difficult to interpret and validate. Explainability techniques provide insight into model decision-making, helping expose errors, failure modes, and potential bias so users can decide whether to rely on model outputs. Explanations are simplified approximations of a language model's internal workings. The goal is to obtain explanations that reflect the underlying computation as closely as possible (faithfulness), are understandable to users (plausibility), and help them achieve their intended goals (utility). Evaluation protocols are essential for assessing these dimensions. This thesis studies highlight explanations, natural language explanations, and chain-of-thought reasoning. These forms offer complementary perspectives on model behaviour and exhibit distinct strengths and limitations across tasks. Producing explanations that satisfy multiple quality dimensions remains challenging, as does evaluating them reliably across forms and settings. This thesis aims to improve people's understanding of models' decision-making processes in complex reasoning tasks. First, it proposes two evaluation frameworks for assessing highlight explanations across multiple properties and explanation types, together with a meta-evaluation framework for examining the reliability of existing faithfulness metrics for chain-of-thought explanations. Second, it proposes two techniques that generate natural language explanations designed to be faithful to the model's prediction process while remaining concise, coherent, and helpful for understanding model decisions. Finally, a study of human-AI interaction explores the roles of evidence and explanations in helping users validate model verdicts in a fact-checking setting.

paper.title: Limite 1B - Violetto: Technical Report
paper.abstract: We present Limite 1B - Violetto, a one-billion-parameter model designed for high-throughput mathematical reasoning. Limite is trained from scratch on 237 billion tokens from a carefully curated, mathematics-centric corpus and supports context lengths of up to 131k tokens. Its architecture and training recipe were developed together to maximize reasoning capability while keeping training and inference costs low. Post-training combines knowledge distillation, targeted supervised fine-tuning, and RLVR on a curated curriculum. Limite achieves 94.01% on AIME 2026 and 74.25% on BeyondAIME, placing it among models many times its size on our evaluation suite. The model is deliberately only lightly instruction-tuned: it is intended primarily as a single-turn mathematical solver and as a fast, parallel component of larger systems, rather than as a general-purpose assistant. We release the model, its base and value checkpoints, and an optimized serving implementation under the Apache 2.0 license.

paper.title: PGPO: Prototype-Guided Progressive Obfuscation for Privacy-Preserving LLM-Enhanced Recommendation
paper.abstract: LLM-enhanced recommender systems encode item side information into semantic embeddings, but these embeddings may leak sensitive textual attributes through inversion attacks. Existing input-side defenses rely on trusted collection or local token perturbation, often disrupting the inter-item semantic topology needed for recommendation. To address it, we introduce relational fidelity as the key objective, requiring semantic shift for privacy while preserving relative item relations for utility. Based on this principle, we propose prototype-guided progressive obfuscation (PGPO), which learns topology-aware obfuscation anchors for high-influence prototype words and propagates them through a static semantic graph. PGPO is optimized with GRPO using individual dissimilarity, structural consistency, and semantic constraint rewards. Experiments on two benchmarks show strong inversion defense with near-upper-bound recommendation performance. The code is available at https://github.com/Shengxiang-Lin/PGPO.

paper.title: HireWatch: Evaluating LLM Compliance with U.S. Employment Law Under Contextual Pressure
paper.abstract: The deployment of large language models (LLMs) in hiring pipelines is growing, yet existing evaluations generally overlook their compliance with legal rules. To fill this gap, we introduce HireWatch, an evaluation that assesses whether LLMs comply with U.S. laws that govern the questions that job candidates may be asked. We construct a 200-item bank of lawful and unlawful interview questions, whose legal classification is based on U.S. federal statutes, regulations, and agency guidance. We instruct LLMs to select questions from this bank in preparing for job interviews, across a set of various occupations and contexts, and report the fraction of unlawful questions that LLMs select. Evaluation of 18 closed and open-weight LLMs across ~100,000 trials under different types of contextual pressure reveals that LLMs' legal compliance is brittle. While LLMs generally avoid selecting unlawful questions in low-pressure contexts, legal violations increase sharply under higher pressure. Explicit prompts to comply with law can improve compliance rates, but do not altogether eliminate legal violations. We publicly release our code and data at https://github.com/hnghiem-nlp/hirewatch_repo.

paper.title: Global Importance Estimation for KV Cache Eviction
paper.abstract: Memory consumption of the key-value (KV) cache remains a central bottleneck for long-context LLM inference. We introduce PRKV, a training-free KV eviction method that estimates multi-hop global token importance by applying Personalized PageRank over attention-induced transition graphs. This enables importance propagation beyond recency or instantaneous attention, without modifying the model. We benchmark PRKV on long-context understanding, sparse retrieval, and chain-of-thought reasoning tasks using multiple LLM families. Under moderate to aggressive compression ratios, including up to 90%, PRKV achieves competitive task performance against established eviction baselines while reducing peak memory usage with low end-to-end overhead. These results demonstrate that multi-hop global influence estimation yields a favorable accuracy--memory trade-off for scalable long-context inference.

paper.title: Token Commitment as a Control Surface for Steering Masked Diffusion Generation
paper.abstract: Masked diffusion models repeatedly predict provisional tokens before a sampler decides which predictions become permanent. Existing inference-time steering methods primarily modify activations, logits, or denoising trajectories, while treating this commitment policy as a fixed decoding detail. We instead study token commitment as a diffusion-specific control surface and separate it into two decisions: which tokens to commit and how many tokens to commit at each step. For the first, we introduce counterfactual target-aware commitment, which ranks unresolved positions by a mixture of model confidence and leave-one-token-out target contribution. For the second, we introduce calibrated adaptive budgets driven by target progress and confidence. Across language and vision-language settings in the LLaDA family, multiple targets, two activation-steering methods, and an unsteered control, both mechanisms yield empirically monotonic target-quality trade-offs in every configuration we evaluate. Adaptive schedules also recover competitive operating points relative to scorer-free stochastic schedules matched in average denoising cost. Because both mechanisms require only a scalar score evaluated on a provisional completion, they apply unchanged when the target is an automatic proxy for task success rather than an output attribute: NLI entailment for dialogue summarization and CLIPScore for captioning, neither of which corresponds to a single reusable steering direction. We reproduce the behavior of both mechanisms on a second masked-diffusion family, Dream-7B, for one control target and one task-success target. These results characterize commitment--which provisional predictions become irreversible, and how rapidly--as an interpretable control surface for steering masked diffusion generation under the conditions we test.

paper.title: From Preference Data to Personalization: Tracing Sycophancy in Large Language Models
paper.abstract: Sycophancy in large language models is often measured as agreement with the user, yet agreement can be appropriate when the user's claim is valid, their preference is genuine, or their experience warrants acknowledgment. We study sycophancy as inappropriate agreement: validating a claim, preference, or self-assessment when the context calls for correction, qualification, or resistance. We introduce a validity-aware sycophancy grader and SycoDrift, a persona-targeted evaluation set of 3,298 validity-annotated probes with controlled annotations for user openness and stakes. We use this framework to analyze three sources of agreement pressure: human preference data, automated judge specification, and in-context personalization. First, preference for validating responses in human datasets (Chatbot Arena, HH-RLHF, Community Alignment) is weak and concentrated where agreement is often appropriate. Second, in a selected-value, single-model experiment, emphasized judge rubrics produce consistent but modest increases relative to paired suppressed rubrics, demonstrating a plausible mechanism for training-time amplification. Third, in off-policy evaluations across 14 models, inference-time personalization increases inappropriate agreement, with the largest effect from matched user profiles placed directly before the query.

paper.title: Benchmarking and Adapting LLMs for English-Swedish Medical Question Answering
paper.abstract: Large language models do well on English medical exams, but less is known about Swedish. This matters most for small open models that hospitals can run locally. To reduce this gap, we first build an item-aligned English-Swedish benchmark from ten medical multiple-choice datasets; each Swedish item keeps the options and answer of its English source. A conservative refinement loop repairs the translations: open models from three families find errors, ground them in a Swedish medical term base, and keep a model-written edit only if blind judges vote for it. On this benchmark, small models lose much more accuracy in Swedish than large ones, especially when they answer without reasoning. Second, we ask whether English data and open teacher models can close this gap. We translate the training data, let teachers write reasoning traces, and fine-tune two small students on gold answers or traces in English, Swedish, or both. Training on reasoning traces that include Swedish closes the gap and lifts the 1.2B student from 23.5\% to 52.0\% in Swedish, slightly above a 20B open model in its fast mode, with a sixth of its memory. We release the benchmark, its edit history, and the code.
